title: Mechanisms & rate-determining step
examples: How do we figure out the rate law from a mechanism?
Is the rate-determining step always the slowest step?
What is the relationship between the mechanism and the overall rate equation?

explain.say: A reaction mechanism describes the steps of a chemical reaction.
Each step in the mechanism is called an elementary step.
The overall rate law comes from the slowest elementary step.
The stoichiometry of the rate-determining step gives the rate law.
Consider the reaction $\text{A} + \text{B} \rightarrow \text{Products}$ through two steps.
In the real world, think about how a car brakes suddenly.

faq.q: Does the rate law always match the stoichiometry?
faq.a: No, the rate law is determined by the stoichiometry of the slowest step.
asks: Will the overall equation rate law match?
Does the rate law follow the balanced equation?

faq.q: What happens if all steps are fast?
faq.a: If all steps are fast, the reaction rate is controlled by the step with the highest activation energy.
asks: Can there be no rate-determining step?
If rates are similar, which step matters most?

faq.q: Are intermediates always reactants or products?
faq.a: Intermediates are species formed and then consumed within the reaction mechanism.
asks: What are intermediates in a reaction?
Are intermediates visible in the final equation?

faq.q: How do we prove the rate-determining step?
faq.a: We often use experimental data or advanced theoretical calculations to identify the slowest step.
asks: Is there a way to measure the slowest step?
How do we know which step is rate-limiting?

faq.q: Does the rate law change if we change temperature?
faq.a: Changing temperature affects the rate constants for all steps, but the rate law structure remains based on the slow step.
asks: Does temperature affect the rate law exponents?
How does temperature affect the rate-determining step?

facts: The rate-determining step is the slowest elementary step in the reaction mechanism.
The rate law derived from the mechanism must match the experimentally determined rate law.
Intermediates are species present only within the reaction mechanism.
The stoichiometry of the rate-determining step dictates the form of the rate law.

quiz.say: If the first step is $\text{A} + \text{B} \rightarrow \text{I}$ and this is slow, what is the rate law?
quiz.why: The rate law is determined by the stoichiometry of the slow step, which is A plus B.

wrong.0: This includes the intermediate [I], which is not in the initial reactants.
wrong.1: This incorrectly uses the stoichiometry from the overall reaction.
wrong.3: This incorrectly adds the concentrations instead of multiplying them.

quiz.say: In a multi-step reaction, what does the rate law reflect?

options.show: The stoichiometry of the slowest step.
options.say: The stoichiometry of the slowest step.

options.show: The overall stoichiometry of all steps combined.
options.say: The overall stoichiometry of all steps combined.

options.show: The rate law from the fastest step.
options.say: The rate law from the fastest step.

options.show: The rate law derived from collision theory.
options.say: The rate law derived from collision theory.

quiz.why: The rate law must be derived directly from the balanced equation of the rate-determining step.

wrong.1: The overall stoichiometry is not always the rate-determining step.
wrong.2: The fastest step does not control the overall speed of the reaction.
wrong.3: Collision theory explains rate factors but does not provide the specific rate law structure.

quiz.say: If the slow step is $\text{C} \rightarrow \text{D} + \text{E}$, what is the rate law?
quiz.why: The rate law matches the reactants in the slow step, which is only C.

wrong.0: The rate law cannot depend on products formed in the slow step.
wrong.1: This assumes the slow step involves two molecules of C reacting.
wrong.2: Rates are proportional to concentrations, not sums of concentrations.
